whyItExists.problem: Browsers render text in a default serif font at a fixed size. Real designs require custom typefaces, readable line lengths, and a clear visual hierarchy.
whyItExists.solution: CSS typography properties control every aspect of text: the font family, size, weight, line height, letter spacing, alignment, and decoration.
whyItExists.whenToUse: On every project. Typography is the foundation of readable, professional-looking interfaces.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Text itself — the words — belongs in HTML. CSS only controls how it looks, not what it says.

explainModes.beginner: Typography CSS is how you tell the browser which font to use, how big to make it, how thick the letters are, and how much space to put between lines.
explainModes.simple: font-family picks the typeface, font-size sets the size, font-weight controls boldness, and line-height sets vertical spacing between lines. text-align positions text left, right, or centre.
explainModes.standard: font-family accepts a comma-separated list of fonts — the browser uses the first one available, falling back to the next. font-size is typically set in rem (relative to root) for scalability. line-height should be unitless (1.5) rather than a fixed px value so it scales with font-size.
explainModes.technical: CSS fonts work via the @font-face rule or the Google Fonts API. The font shorthand packs font-style, font-variant, font-weight, font-size/line-height, and font-family into one declaration. Variable fonts (a single file containing many weights/widths) are now widely supported and dramatically reduce font payload.
explainModes.deepDive: The CSS Fonts Module Level 4 adds font-display (controlling flash-of-unstyled-text behaviour), font-variation-settings for variable font axes, and optical sizing. The text rendering pipeline: Unicode codepoints → font glyphs (via font matching) → layout (shaping, kerning, ligatures via HarfBuzz) → rasterisation. font-kerning, font-feature-settings, and text-rendering: optimizeLegibility enable OpenType features like ligatures and alternates.

content.text: Use unitless line-height (e.g. 1.5) not 24px. A unitless value multiplies the element's own font-size, so it scales correctly when the font-size changes.

questions.question: What font-weight value represents 'bold'?
questions.explanation: font-weight: 700 is the standard 'bold' weight. 400 is regular/normal. 900 is extra-black. Many fonts only have 400 and 700 available.

questions.question: Why is unitless line-height (e.g. 1.6) better than a fixed px value?
options: It scales proportionally when font-size changes
It is the only valid syntax
questions.explanation: A unitless line-height multiplies the element's own font-size. If you later change font-size from 16px to 20px, line-height adjusts automatically. A fixed 24px value would not scale.

faq.q: What is the difference between em and rem for font sizes?
faq.a: em is relative to the parent element's font-size. rem is relative to the root (<html>) font-size (usually 16px). rem is easier to reason about because it does not compound through nested elements.

faq.q: How do I load custom fonts?
faq.a: Use Google Fonts: add <link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Inter..." rel="stylesheet"> to your <head>, then set font-family: 'Inter', sans-serif in CSS. For self-hosted fonts, use @font-face with the font file URLs.

faq.q: How many fonts should I use on a page?
faq.a: One to two font families is usually enough. One for body text, optionally one for headings or code. Every additional font family is an extra network request.
